talks.title: Keynote: Building Leadership, 1% at a Time
talks.teaser: Argues everyone leads and offers practical habits on wellness, inclusion and alignment to stop wasting team energy.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that leadership is not a job title. Ellis argues that everyone leads through influence, and that most leaders unintentionally destroy value by wasting the energy their people bring to work. He describes six ways this happens: exhausting staff, excluding them, getting work they are unwilling to do, assigning work they cannot do, producing ineffective results, and pulling against the wider organisation's direction.

He groups the remedies into wellness, inclusion, inspiration, development, planning and alignment, and applies each at the individual, team and organisational level. Examples include ending long incident shifts after eight hours with a fresh team, tracking whether staff actually use their vacation, and assuming good intent when a colleague causes friction. He also covers small everyday inclusions, celebrating finished security fixes, involving teams in hard decisions, giving feedback by describing evidence and impact before suggesting changes, and building development plans for the middle of a team rather than only the top performers and those being managed out. Planning is framed around preparedness and flexibility, and alignment around a shared vision and keeping oversight of processes.

He closes by encouraging listeners to find their weakest leadership skill and improve it by about one percent each day, since small gains compound. The talk suits anyone who manages people or wants to lead without a formal role.

talks.title: Keynote
talks.teaser: Offers a keynote drawing on security program building, penetration testing and vulnerability management experience.

talks.title: A programmatic approach to enterprise security
talks.teaser: Argues that enterprise security should run as a continuous, business-driven program rather than annual checkbox testing.
talks.summary:
Luke McOmie opens by polling the audience on why they run security programs, assessments and penetration tests. Common answers such as compliance requirements, insurance demands and once-a-year testing become the starting point for his critique. He argues that yearly provider changes, reliance on vulnerability scan dashboards and opaque risk scorecards give leaders a false sense of coverage while losing the depth that comes from knowing an environment over time.

The middle of the talk covers firefighting, one-off projects and cyber insurance used as a substitute for protection. McOmie describes how executives are more likely to fund security work when it is framed in financial and operational terms, such as the cost of remediation and the return on the effort, rather than in severity ratings or fear of reputational damage. He recommends learning how the business makes money before discussing technology, bringing people from across departments into a security council, and cross-mapping overlapping compliance requirements into a single readiness assessment. He is also skeptical of zero trust sales pitches for organizations without large budgets or specialized staff.

The closing section steps back to a practical takeaway: treat security as a living, continuous process, prioritize work by its impact on the business, and avoid adopting industry defaults without checking them against your own environment. He gives the example of a low-rated SMB signing finding that testers often use early in an engagement. The talk ends with an invitation to continue the conversation informally and a short personal note.

talks.title: Why You Can't Call the Police
talks.teaser: Traces a stolen NFT theft from blockchain transactions to a real suspect, and shows why police often cannot act on it.
talks.summary:
The talk follows an investigator at a law firm who was asked to recover NFTs stolen from a client who had hardened his accounts and said he had clicked nothing suspicious. The first step was reading the blockchain. The assets moved through a chain of burner wallets, were sold on an NFT marketplace, and the proceeds were spread across more wallets before being cashed out at a centralised exchange. Raw ledger data is hard to read without tooling, and a wallet address alone means nothing a court can use.

The team then considered whether a malicious smart contract could have moved the assets without the owner noticing. The talk covers fake minting platforms, functions with misleading names, and how common transfer methods are called once a user approves a request. Open-source searches tied one wallet to a domain name listed in a social media bio. Historical DNS records, a clinic website, family links, and an archived social profile then led to a named suspect, whose details were passed to the law firm for verification.

The second half covers evidence handling. Court exhibits must be printable, so screenshots need page numbers, URLs, and capture times, and a documented chain of custody shows who collected and handled each item. Metadata such as GPS data can matter for location-sensitive cases. A campaign collected about nine terabytes over three months, and live streams had to be captured chunk by chunk and converted. AI helped anonymise data before it went to outside tools. The takeaway is that blockchain activity is traceable, but linking it to a person is slow, and police often lack capacity for crypto cases, so user awareness remains the main defence.

talks.title: Network 201: A Tour Through Network Security
talks.teaser: Surveys network protocols, foundational security controls, and how SASE and ZTNA fit into modern remote-access designs.
talks.summary:
Rick Lull revisits a network security primer he first gave in 2019, moving from networking basics into controls and newer remote-access concepts. He opens with a quick review of the OSI layers, common Layer 2 protocols such as VLAN trunking and LLDP, and the transport and routing protocols that carry traffic. He notes how encapsulation and MTU limits can cause hard-to-diagnose failures, such as slow or broken VPN connections.

The middle of the talk shifts from protocols to architecture and risk. Lull argues that networks grown without a plan are hard to protect, so teams should know their assets, identify the business owners who decide how data is used, and remove data they no longer need. He recommends low-cost hardening steps like changing default credentials, disabling unused services, enabling logging, and using CIS benchmarks. He also covers layered defenses including MFA, network access control, segmentation, detection, vendor SLAs, and recovery planning, illustrating them with incidents where the outcome depended on luck.

In the final section he looks at cloud and SaaS responsibility models, the difficulty of inspecting encrypted traffic, web application firewalls, outbound filtering, CASBs, and secure web gateways. He explains that SASE and ZTNA mostly package existing VPN, firewall and proxy functions into a cloud-delivered service. His takeaway is that the right design depends on where users, applications and data actually sit.

talks.title: I ❤️ My Password
talks.teaser: Traces the history of passwords and walks through MFA and passwordless options in Azure AD conditional access.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by describing identity as a pairing of a visible username and a hidden secret, and traces how people have protected access for thousands of years, from ancient locks to early computer passwords. The speaker then looks at how Active Directory's default password policies and later, conflicting guidance on complexity and expiration left users confused and frustrated. Predictable password habits are used as an example of why rotation rules alone do little.

The middle of the talk turns to the present. Figures from Microsoft's digital defense report show multi-factor authentication adoption still lagging, with administrators not much ahead of ordinary users. The speaker explains how Azure AD grew to many authentication methods, which made choices hard for administrators, and how some organisations fell back on weaker federation setups. Legacy systems and the assumption that every worker carries a phone create further barriers, especially for frontline staff.

The practical part covers recent changes: authenticator features built into mobile apps, number matching to resist push fatigue, system-preferred MFA, custom authentication strengths, and conditional access policies that limit access by device, location and method. The speaker suggests reviewing exported policies with a community tool and stresses communication, education and user participation over forced change. The takeaway is that identity controls have to account for the people who use them, and that the tooling is still maturing.

talks.title: Cybernation: The FUD, Facts, & Future of Software Liability/Security
talks.teaser: Explains how courts, regulators and corporate law already hold software makers liable for security failures.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the 2023 National Cybersecurity Strategy and its proposal to move liability onto software makers, which the speaker argues is less novel than the online reaction suggested. Software liability is treated here as several distinct legal strands: contract terms that divide risk between vendors and customers, regulatory enforcement, corporate governance claims, criminal fines, and tort law. Each strand is illustrated with a concrete case or agency example.

Examples include FDA software recalls, a Delaware shareholder case involving Meta's board, a criminal fine tied to Volkswagen's emissions defeat device, and design-defect suits against Snapchat and TikTok that got past early dismissal motions. The history runs from 1980s medical device failures and Y2K through to Centralia, Pennsylvania, whose underground mine fire is used as a warning about systems whose interactions no one anticipated.

For practitioners, the main takeaways are that courts and regulators weigh duty, intent to engage in the conduct that caused harm, and the promises a company made publicly. The speaker advises employees to keep their own records of security decisions and to build trusted allies inside the organization. She proposes extending threat models with social sustainability, substantiation of design choices, and non-technical stakeholders, and closes by calling for a technology regulator of last resort.

talks.title: TOP 5 CISO FINDINGS OF 2022
talks.teaser: Walks through five recurring security gaps seen across client engagements and how to map them to a framework.
talks.summary:
Mark Arnold of Lares presents the top five findings his advisory team recorded across client work in 2022, drawn from virtual CISO, risk assessment, offensive testing and program management engagements. He explains that the list reflects how often each issue appeared rather than how severe it was, and that the clients ranged from mid-market firms to critical infrastructure operators. The countdown begins with weak asset management, followed by gaps in vulnerability scanning and timely patching, then blind spots caused by missing logs and monitoring.

The talk moves on to insecure default and extraneous configurations, which attackers know well and can exploit easily, and to the lack of current data flow diagrams that would make unusual traffic stand out. Arnold uses the Capital One breach, as analysed in an MIT Sloan case study, to connect these issues. A misconfigured web application firewall let the attacker reach instance metadata, retrieve credentials, and copy cloud storage buckets, with each step tied to one of the findings.

For remediation, he recommends choosing a recognised framework such as NIST CSF, mapping existing controls and gaps against it, and then designing tactical tests for each function instead of relying on a generic yearly penetration test. He points toward continuous, scripted validation, ranking and quantifying risk with a method such as FAIR, and repeating threat modelling afterward. His closing point is that buying more tools rarely fixes these gaps, and that the people operating them and the validation of existing controls matter more.

talks.title: Cyber, the Commonwealth and You
talks.teaser: Virginia's deputy homeland security secretary explains the state's cyber roles, workforce pipeline, and why incidents must be reported.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by Virginia's deputy secretary of homeland security, argues that cybercrime is not limited to technology targets and affects every resident, from hospitals and 911 systems to schools and small family farms. The speaker walks through FBI complaint figures, noting that phishing losses look modest next to romance and tech-support scams, which hit older residents hardest. The speaker also stresses that underreporting likely hides much of the real picture.

The middle of the talk maps the state's response as a shared effort. The state police fusion center collects incident reports, and its high-tech crimes unit investigates alongside the FBI, the Virginia National Guard, the state IT agency, and emergency management. A new state cyber annex defines who takes the lead as an incident grows, and recent legislation asks localities to report incidents within 24 hours, although the definition of a reportable incident remained unclear.

The closing section focuses on the workforce gap, citing a large number of unfilled cyber jobs and a move to drop degree requirements for many state roles. Schools are introducing security basics in elementary grades, with coding activities, student competitions, and a cyber range open to students and teachers. The question period covered federal funding for localities and the need for industry partnerships. The main takeaway is that residents and organizations should report incidents to the Virginia Fusion Center and support local education and internship efforts.

talks.title: Who Goes There? Actively Detecting Intruders w/Cyber Deception Tools
talks.teaser: Explains honey tokens as decoy credentials that raise alarms when intruders use them, with AWS build examples and tool options.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a run of recent breaches, including a CI platform compromise, a ride-sharing company intrusion, a car maker's exposed key and a pharmaceutical firm's leaked test credentials. The speaker argues that most attackers are financially motivated, through ransomware and cryptomining, and that stolen credentials are the common thread. Since perimeter defenses will eventually fail, the focus shifts to catching intruders quickly once they are inside.

The speaker traces deception tools from early honeypots through to honey tokens, which are decoy credentials with no real access that trigger an alert and reveal an IP address when used. One approach on AWS creates an unused user, sends its activity from CloudTrail into S3, and uses a Lambda function to match events against the decoy list and send notifications. Open-source and commercial options were mentioned, including Canarytoken, GG Canary and Space Siren. Practical tips included keeping tokens in private locations, making them look realistic, placing one token across many repositories, and blocking the source IPs or user agents seen during an alert.

The closing section stresses fast detection and response, and warns against using attack tools on systems you do not own. It recommends managed secret stores such as HashiCorp Vault, Doppler or Keyless over plain-text files or environment files, ideally with a security team handling automatic rotation.

talks.title: Beyond the pandemic: How it shaped organizations and their sec architecture
talks.teaser: Explores how a university security leader reshaped access controls around identity and device signals after the pandemic.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker, who leads security at a university, looking back over about twenty years of IT change. The traditional model relied on a trusted internal network behind perimeter firewalls, with VPN access as the drawbridge. Cloud services, bring-your-own-device policies and DevOps gradually weakened that boundary, and the pandemic pushed most users and equipment outside it almost overnight. Organizations made fast, imperfect fixes, and the speaker argues that the resulting shortcuts are now coming due.

To show the cost of those shortcuts, the speaker walks through a password manager breach that began with a remote engineer's unpatched home media server. The central argument is that identity, device posture, location and behavior now form the perimeter, and that authorization should be re-evaluated continuously as those signals change. Practical guidance covers classifying assets, threat modeling the most critical ones, and choosing controls by asset tier so they stay manageable. The speaker also advises keeping exceptions to a minimum, using host-based firewalls, and considering cloud-delivered access services or full-tunnel VPN to give remote users a consistent experience.

The closing message is that security controls should be tied to the business mission and to realistic funding. Simpler access paths, such as relaxing prompts for trusted devices, can improve both protection and user adoption. The talk ends with an invitation for questions.

talks.title: The state of NIST/CMMC compliance today
talks.teaser: Explains NIST 800-171 and CMMC requirements for businesses handling federal contract information, from scoping to audits.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) and the NIST 800-171 standard matter to businesses that work with the federal government, particularly in Virginia, where that work is a major industry. The speaker outlines how contract clauses protect federal contract information and controlled unclassified information, and how those requirements flow down to subcontractors several tiers removed. Breach reporting within 72 hours is highlighted as a duty that can apply well beyond the direct contract holder.

The middle section traces how the false claims case involving Aerojet Rocketdyne pushed the Defense Department toward third-party audits. The speaker covers the SPRS scoring system, which already affects whether firms win deals, and the 110 controls behind NIST 800-171. Scoping is explained as a way to limit audit burden by separating systems that handle controlled information from those that do not. A recent draft revision is described as turning previously assumed practices into explicit requirements. The speaker argues that management buy-in and engagement with customers and suppliers should come before technical work, and notes that the standard addresses confidentiality rather than business continuity.

The closing portion covers audit and remediation costs, the risk of trading compliance work against other security projects, and the expense of duplicating cloud environments for export-controlled data. The speaker recommends GRC tooling, free government training and threat information, and legal review. The main takeaway is that compliance is a business program built on policies, governance and clear ownership across the organisation, not only an IT project.

talks.title: This is the Way: A New Leadership Creed for Info-Sec professionals
talks.teaser: Presents a leadership creed for info-sec professionals, using The Mandalorian to illustrate principles for leading people and teams.
talks.summary:
Kate Collins opens by describing how much the security field has absorbed in recent years, from the pandemic and supply chain strain to burnout and heavy turnover. She argues that cyber professionals lack leadership development tailored to their work, and she cites research on stress, retention and human-driven incidents. In her view, workplace culture and how managers treat their people now decide which employers keep their talent.

The core of the talk is a proposed set of guiding principles, illustrated with episodes from The Mandalorian. The principles cover shifting from an individual focus to a collective one, treating colleagues in the way they prefer, and concentrating on shared outcomes rather than hours or visible presence. Other points include building diverse alliances through empathy, recognising how personal experience and bias shape behaviour, balancing determination with work-life balance, admitting limits and asking for feedback, and keeping the mission in view to avoid burnout.

Collins closes by urging attendees to choose one small change from these ideas and apply it at work, and she points to a worksheet-based resource for setting development goals. For practitioners, the takeaway is that skills such as communication, self-awareness and humility are a practical part of staying effective in security roles.

talks.title: Insiders packing their bags with your data
talks.teaser: Shows how behavioral analytics and DLP signals reveal employees moving corporate data to personal cloud apps before leaving.
talks.summary:
Colin Estep opens with a hypothetical employee who gradually copies project files, guides and source code to personal cloud storage during a job search. The talk argues that data theft by departing staff is common, often not malicious, and that organizations need to spot it while the person is still employed rather than after they leave.

Drawing on data from more than 200 organizations over roughly nine months, covering about 58,000 people who left, Estep reports that a modest share moved data to personal apps and a smaller share violated corporate policy. Intellectual property and personal data made up most of what was taken, Google services were the dominant destination, and much of the movement happened weeks before notice was given. He walks through three signals: the direction of data movement, the nature of the data using DLP labels and policies, and its volume. Baselines are built at user, peer group and organization levels with anomaly models that flag spikes and first-time or rare behavior, and the talk covers how these models are deployed, tuned and triaged. Case studies show a confirmed departure, a likely leak and a benign case.

The takeaway for practitioners is to monitor a rolling window of roughly 50 days, combine direction, data sensitivity and volume rather than relying on simple thresholds, and invest in tuning so that alert review stays manageable.

talks.title: Corporate Dungeon Master: How to Lead Cyber Games at Work
talks.teaser: Shows how to run tabletop incident response exercises at work using Dungeons and Dragons style facilitation and planning.
talks.summary:
This talk presents the cyber action officer role, a job many companies have only recently created, as similar to a Dungeon Master's. The speaker, who moved from threat intelligence and government contracting into this position at a financial institution, explains that much of the work is running tabletop exercises rather than managing live crises. He gives a short primer on Dungeons and Dragons for attendees who have not played, covering character creation, dice, and the game master's job of narrating the story and controlling non-player characters.

The middle of the talk maps the game onto exercise design. Preparation resembles a session zero: citing existing policies and architecture documents, drawing realistic threats from past incidents and public breach reports, and building a stakeholder group around a senior executive sponsor who owns the exercise and steers discussion. The scenario is laid out in a master scenario events list of injects, with a short overview written early. During delivery, the facilitator keeps the scenario close to real processes, stays ready to improvise when participants push the plot somewhere unexpected, manages the clock, and records sessions to support note-taking.

The talk closes with aftercare. After an exercise, the facilitator collects feedback, writes an after-action report, and holds a review meeting where gaps become process improvement opportunities, each with a named owner. The speaker notes that roughly 90-minute sessions work well and that the same approach suits cross-functional collaboration exercises. The takeaway for practitioners is a structure for planning, running, and following up on exercises that involve senior leaders.

talks.title: Hacking your Job? Trying to cheat at life with ChatGPT
talks.teaser: Explores where ChatGPT adds value to security roles like threat modeling and reporting, and where it fails or gets jailbroken.
talks.summary:
David Girvin, who comes from application security and now works in sales engineering, frames this session as a practical test of whether ChatGPT is hype or useful for security work. He treats the model like an offensive security lab and reports trying many approaches over several months, noting how its behavior shifted as the vendor patched it.

On the job side, he generates a baseline threat model for a typical web stack, then shows how follow-up prompts and supplied context drill it deeper. He also covers drafting policy from that model, rewriting penetration test reports, summarizing threat intelligence, and preparing quick research for customer conversations. A code review of a script returned findings within seconds, though he cautions against pasting secrets or proprietary code. He demonstrates guardrails: a direct request for malware was refused, but reframing it as personal file encryption produced usable scripting, and a phishing example followed. He also raises concerns about data handling and vendor transparency.

He closes by arguing that people who learn these tools will outpace those who do not, and that routine tasks will be automated while interpersonal work grows in importance. His suggestion is to list the tasks you dislike most, test the model on them, and share what works with peers.

talks.title: Heap Exploitation from First Principles
talks.teaser: Builds a userland heap allocator step by step and shows how its design flaws can be exploited.
talks.summary:
Kevin Massey explains why someone might write a userland heap allocator from scratch. A stripped-down version makes the mechanics of production allocators easier to follow, and it supports vulnerability research because custom allocators tend to repeat the bug classes of well-known ones. He illustrates the point with a glibc flaw documented in 2001, believed fixed the following year, and not found again until 2018.

He walks through a simple allocator with inline headers holding a size, a next pointer, a free flag and a magic value, covering allocation, freeing and chunk reuse. A heap overflow that rewrites a neighbouring header's next pointer makes a later allocation return a stack address, which lets him overwrite a function pointer in a jump table so the program calls a different function. He then extends the design with fast bins, which behave as last-in-first-out stacks for small fixed sizes, plus sorted doubly linked bins for larger chunks, along with 8-byte alignment, an arena and a top chunk.

The final section covers a use-after-free against fast bins, where an overwritten forward pointer makes a later allocation return an attacker-chosen target. Massey notes that heap exploits can also corrupt data or global offset table entries, and that a clean exploit keeps the process running so it goes unnoticed. His main takeaway is that knowing an allocator's intended invariants is the fastest route to finding its flaws.

talks.title: Everything you never knew you wanted to know about Passkeys
talks.teaser: Explains how passkeys replace passwords, sync across devices, and resist phishing, with a live registration demo.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the long-running problem of passwords, which are reused, phished, and exposed in breach collections, and presents passkeys as a replacement. A passkey is a machine-generated public and private key pair. The private half stays with the user and is never shared, while the relying party stores only the public half and verifies a signed challenge. Nothing reusable is kept on the server for attackers to take.

The middle section separates the open standard from vendor implementations such as those from Apple and Google, and explains synced passkeys that move through cloud keychains or password managers versus device-bound credentials. It walks through the WebAuthn and CTAP2 exchange, showing how the requesting origin is bound into each signed response, which is why a proxied login page gets nothing useful. Hybrid transport, which uses a QR code and Bluetooth to register a key on a nearby device, is demonstrated live.

The closing part looks at deployment. Support is now broad across major operating systems and browsers, but uneven in some native apps. The speaker stresses planning for recovery and help desk workflows, knowing the user base, and offering alternatives such as hardware keys for users who cannot use phones. Hardware security keys and passkeys are presented as largely the same kind of authenticator.

talks.title: Quantum Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Explains how quantum computers threaten current encryption and what post-quantum and key distribution options can do about it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the quantum landscape, covering computing, sensing and communications, and argues that large quantum computers would undermine much of today's public-key encryption. The speaker stresses the stakes for finance and critical infrastructure and points to heavy government investment abroad as a reason for urgency.

The middle section reviews cryptography basics, including the gap between schemes proven secure against any computer and those only believed secure against known ones. It explains why true randomness matters, why public-key infrastructure designed decades ago fits poorly with modern cloud networks, and why captured traffic can be stored now and decrypted later. Examples of flawed hardware tokens, compromised certificates and supply chain problems illustrate how long-lived weaknesses persist. Quantum key distribution and a cloud-based quantum entropy approach are compared, with their cost and speed trade-offs.

The closing argument is that organizations should begin migrating to the post-quantum standards now, since legacy systems take years to replace and federal contracts will require compliance. Practical advice includes staying crypto-agile, demanding verifiable end-to-end encryption from vendors, and assigning staff to follow the standards work. Audience questions covered the transmission speed limits of key distribution and how ephemeral keys reduce exposure.

talks.title: Context Matters: Tailoring Tradecraft to the Operational Environment
talks.teaser: Explains how red teamers can tailor offensive tradecraft to a target's environment so their activity blends in with normal behavior.
talks.summary:
Fletcher Davis, a senior red team consultant, argues that offensive operations should be shaped by the specific environment being targeted rather than by a standard penetration testing routine. He opens with a set of foundational principles from a book on network operations, including humanity, access, economy, knowledge, awareness, innovation, precaution, operational security and program security. The core idea is that human habits, biases and business processes create the patterns an operator has to work within.

The middle of the talk covers planning. Davis describes building a target package that maps the host, network, cloud, DevOps and business layers of an organization, then modeling who has access to a sensitive objective such as customer data. One example traced an exposed Spring actuator to internal web applications, a vulnerable Jenkins server and eventually cloud credentials. He then presents a framework for understanding normality, which builds a baseline of benign process behavior from Windows event tracing telemetry so that malicious activity can resemble what a host normally does.

He closes with lean host-based reconnaissance, targeting less monitored systems such as wikis and collaboration platforms, and avoiding unnecessary lateral movement. His takeaways for practitioners are to challenge assumptions, understand the people who run the environment, and treat defensive telemetry as something an operator can also use.

talks.title: Feature or a Vulnerability? Tale of an Active Directory Pentest
talks.teaser: Walks through Active Directory pentest techniques that abuse default Windows features, from name resolution poisoning to Kerberoasting.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a question the speaker says comes up often in penetration test reports: whether a Windows behaviour counts as a feature or a flaw. Microsoft's documentation explains clearly right and wrong configurations, the speaker argues, but says little about the gray area in between. The examples come from recent engagements inside Active Directory networks, and the emphasis is on noisy techniques rather than stealth.

The middle of the talk follows an attack chain. Fallback name resolution over broadcast and multicast lets a tester answer requests and capture NTLM hashes, which can be cracked or relayed to hosts where that account holds local admin. From there, cached credentials, pass-the-hash and pass-the-ticket move the tester between machines. Kerberoasting exposes service account passwords that are often over-privileged, and trust relationships between domains and forests can enable ticket forging. Weak group policy and broad local admin rights round out the examples.

The closing section turns to defence. The speaker recommends disabling NetBIOS and LLMNR, enforcing SMB signing, using AES for Kerberos, moving to managed service accounts, limiting admin rights, and enabling Credential Guard. Honeypot accounts and correlating logons in a SIEM are presented as ways to catch lateral movement, and BloodHound is suggested for mapping attack paths. Changes should be tested first, since hardening can break software.

talks.title: Software Bills of Behaviors: Why SBOMs aren't enough
talks.teaser: Explains why component inventories miss supply chain attacks and how tracking software behavior can close the gap.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the SolarWinds compromise and the 3CX attack, showing how trusted software can be altered after source review and signing. The speaker argues that software bills of materials, which list a product's components, help with compliance but do not reveal what software will actually do once it runs. Because trust is spread across compilers, vendors and open-source dependencies, verification has to be ongoing.

The middle section proposes a software bill of behaviors: a record of network connections, data use, file and host activity, and technique mappings. Behaviors can be gathered by asking vendors, reading open-source code, analyzing binaries, or observing runtime, though developers often lack that visibility. Examples include privacy-label mismatches and a crypto-mining feature that took months to surface. Baselines make unexpected changes between versions stand out, which can cut alert fatigue and inform patching decisions.

The closing part covers scanner noise, such as flagged functions a product never calls, and shows a backdoored Notepad build that launched a calculator without drawing attention. The takeaways are that SBOMs are a baseline rather than a complete answer, that teams should request behavior information from suppliers and build their own baselines, and that security staff should frame these asks around what developers care about.

talks.title: Shakespeare, Bacon, and the NSA
talks.teaser: Traces how a Shakespeare cipher project led a code-breaker into wartime cryptanalysis and the origins of the NSA.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with Francis Bacon's line "knowledge is power" and the story of Elizabeth Smith Friedman, a cryptologist whose career started in the early 1900s at Riverbank, a private research estate in Illinois. She was hired to help check a supposed hidden cipher in the First Folio, a project meant to prove Bacon wrote Shakespeare's plays. There she met William Friedman, and the two came to doubt the theory, while their work on ciphers grew into professional cryptanalysis.

The middle of the talk follows their wartime careers. The Zimmermann Telegram helped push the United States toward World War I, and the Friedmans became central to decoding enemy messages and training other government departments. During Prohibition, Elizabeth worked for the Coast Guard on bootlegging messages and gave testimony in court cases. Before and during World War II she helped expose Nazi spy networks in the Americas, work the FBI often received credit for. William founded the Army Signal Corps, which later evolved into the NSA. After Elizabeth's contributions became public, the NSA renamed an Fort Meade auditorium to honor both of them.

The closing section draws four lessons for modern defenders: work across disciplines, think like an attacker, test and improve security continuously, and speak up when compliance is mistaken for real safety. The speaker links the Friedmans' pattern recognition to today's AI tools and argues that human judgment still matters.

talks.title: Adversary TTP Evolution & the Value of TTP Intelligence
talks.teaser: Shows how ransomware and malware families change their behaviors over time and how TTP intelligence helps defenders keep pace.
talks.summary:
Scott Small opens by separating indicators, such as command-and-control addresses and domains, from adversary behaviors, meaning the tactics, techniques and procedures attackers use. Using a bank robbery comparison, he argues that behaviors are costlier for attackers to swap out, so defending against them imposes more expense. He presents MITRE ATT&CK as a shared vocabulary for classifying and tracking those behaviors.

The middle of the talk reviews recent shifts. An initial access loader and IcedID both changed their delivery methods within weeks after Microsoft tightened protections on downloaded macro documents, moving to other file types and OneNote. Some ransomware groups have dropped encryption in favor of stealing data and threatening to leak it, which is faster and can be detected earlier in the attack chain. Info stealers have gained defense evasion features and now target multi-factor tokens and cookies, while malvertising has grown as a delivery route.

The closing guidance focuses on turning intelligence into action. Small recommends mapping reports to ATT&CK identifiers, then pulling procedure-level details such as commands and process relationships, which are needed for accurate detections and simulations. He cautions that defenders should consider variations of observed techniques rather than only the exact commands from one campaign. He also argues that publishing this kind of reporting benefits the defender community, despite the risk that adversaries may read it.

talks.title: Ransomware Rebranding ... So Hot Right Now!
talks.teaser: Shows how ransomware groups rebrand to dodge law enforcement and how analysts link new identities back to older groups.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the growth of ransomware activity, showing that the number of active groups rose steadily from 2022 into 2023. The speaker, a threat intelligence team lead, argues that many operators run ransomware like a business, timing their activity around cryptocurrency prices and financial incentives. He then introduces a taxonomy that sorts groups into full-time operations, rebrands, splinter groups and ephemeral groups, based on their behavior and capabilities.

The middle of the talk covers why groups rebrand, usually after drawing heavy law enforcement attention or damaging publicity, and what the move gains them. Case studies trace one group through several names with shrinking gaps between rebrands, and another whose overlapping variants suggested simultaneous operations. A separate case linked two groups only through a shared email address, found after intelligence sharing with the FBI, despite little similarity in their encryptors. Attribution methods include comparing recurring code routines and coding style, along with behavioral signals such as initial access techniques, negotiation patterns, payment handling and relationships between groups. The speaker cautions that leaked builders and freelance developers can produce false attributions.

The closing section recommends maintaining a living threat profile and sharing intelligence with internal teams in a prioritized, consumable form, then feeding findings into threat models and hunting. Defensive advice centers on a tested incident response plan and fundamentals such as endpoint detection and layered defenses. The takeaway is that collaboration with peers, information sharing groups and law enforcement is how defenders can raise the cost of rebranding.
